questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a conservation act left out
questions.learningObjective: Identify the interest a conservation act excluded from protection
questions.stem: Your survey protocol notes that a wetland was made a protected area, but the statute lists birds and their nests alone among the protected features. What is left out of protection?

options.text: The wetland habitat and the local fishing communities' rights, since only birds were named
Only the birds were protected, so the reed beds and shallow pools were left entirely free
options.misconception: reads a partial protection list as total protection

options.text: Nesting birds were protected but their food and the water they feed in were excluded
options.misconception: focuses on habitat without noticing it was omitted

options.text: The statute excluded every landowner within two miles of the wetland boundary
options.misconception: invents an exclusion the statute never lists

questions.explanation: A statute that names only birds and nests protects those animals, not the reed beds and pools they need, and it leaves existing fishing grants untouched. Protection therefore covers less than a survey team assumes.
questions.hint: Ask what else depends on the water itself.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A park act read as a mechanism
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a park statute creates protection on the ground
questions.stem: Draft a section for the reserve's management plan explaining how a park statute turns into actual protection on the ground.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that a statute works through four linked mechanisms: a drawn boundary, a prohibition on specified acts, a staff or ranger presence that enforces it, and a funding line that pays for both. It also notes that without boundaries and enforcement the text is nominal, and that land rights inside the boundary must be settled before protection can be real.

questions.explanation: A park statute protects only through a boundary, a prohibition, an enforcing staff and a budget. A good answer names all four links and says which one is usually weakest.
questions.hint: A statute needs people and money, not just words.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An agreement with no mechanism behind it
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a signed agreement can operate without finished terms

stimulus.body: A treaty register records that fourteen states signed an agreement on migratory species. The entry lists the signing date, an entry into force date and a deposit of instruments by nine states, and states that the species list and the reporting form are still marked to be agreed.

questions.stem: Your monitoring log for the protected area records that the treaty above has no completed species list. What follows?

options.text: The agreement is legally complete but unusable, since its species list can be added later
options.misconception: treats signing as completion of the obligations

options.text: The agreement protects every migratory species until the list is finally agreed
options.misconception: assumes an empty list still covers all species

options.text: The agreement has no operative species list, so it cannot yet protect anything specific
The agreement failed because nine deposits were fewer than the fourteen signatures
options.misconception: confuses a deposit threshold with a simple headcount

questions.explanation: A treaty that still marks its species list and forms to be agreed has no defined content to enforce, however many states have signed. Deposits may have brought it into force, but force without content does little.
questions.hint: Look at what the register says is still unfinished.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A conference that produced only a declaration
questions.learningObjective: Identify the chief weakness in a conference declaration

stimulus.body: A conference resolution declares that all member governments will protect migratory species across their territories and that a standing committee will meet annually to review progress. The resolution sets no reporting form, no deadline and no agreed list of species.

questions.stem: Your briefing pack quotes the conference resolution above. What is the chief weakness of the text?

options.text: It commits governments to a committee that meets only once each year
options.misconception: treats an annual meeting as a weakness in itself

options.text: It asks too much of governments by extending protection to every territory
options.misconception: blames the scope of the promise rather than its machinery

options.text: It fails to mention migratory species at the top of the document
options.misconception: judges a document by where its subject appears

options.text: It states an intention without any mechanism to check whether it is carried out

questions.explanation: A declaration binds governments in words, but the resolution sets no reporting, deadline or species list, so nothing can be checked or enforced. Meeting frequency and the length of the promise are not the real defect.
questions.hint: Ask how anyone would know whether it was done.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The commitment mechanism of a climate treaty
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a climate treaty obliges states to act
questions.stem: Your carbon accounting sheet asks how a climate treaty actually obliges a state to reduce emissions. Draft the explanation.

options.text: Each state sets its own target, reports against it, and must strengthen it on a fixed cycle
The treaty fixes a single emissions level for every state, weighted by population
options.misconception: confuses national pledges with a single uniform quota

options.text: Inspectors visit each state every year and fine it if targets are not met
options.misconception: invents an inspection and penalty regime that is absent

options.text: The treaty relies on courts in one country to enforce the targets of all others
options.misconception: assumes one state's courts can enforce an international target

questions.explanation: The working mechanism is nationally set targets that must be reported on and then strengthened, so the obligation runs through domestic plans and a regular cycle. Uniform quotas, foreign inspection and court enforcement are not how it works.
questions.hint: Find the repeating cycle in the obligations.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commitment and its revision
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a revised commitment differs from the original
questions.stem: Your monitoring notes for the treaty record that the first commitment period asked each state to reach a target by 2020, and that a later protocol asked for a stronger target by 2030. What changed?

options.text: The deadline was extended, so the same target could be reached later instead of sooner
options.misconception: reads the new date as a delay of the same obligation

options.text: The obligation became stronger and later, adding a new target rather than moving one
The state's freedom to set its own target was removed by the later protocol
options.misconception: invents a change in how targets are set

options.text: The first period's target was declared invalid, so only the later one counts
options.misconception: treats an additional commitment as a cancellation

questions.explanation: A later protocol that asks for a stronger target by a later date adds an obligation on top of the earlier one rather than moving it. The first target is neither extended nor cancelled by the second.
questions.hint: Ask whether the earlier duty disappeared.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the new cereal varieties required
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the new cereal varieties required farmers to change
questions.stem: Write a short explanation for the district office of what the new cereal varieties required farmers to change.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that the new varieties were bred to respond heavily to fertiliser and irrigation and to mature quickly, so they demanded timely inputs, credit for fertiliser and a market for a uniform grain. It adds that they displaced landraces adapted to poor soil and low input, which shifted risk onto farmers with the least cash and left a single dependence on bought seed and fertiliser.

questions.explanation: The new varieties needed water, fertiliser, bought seed and a uniform grain market, so they shifted risk onto farmers with little cash. A good answer names those inputs and the dependence they created.
questions.hint: Ask what a farmer must now buy before planting.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A trial of two varieties
questions.learningObjective: State what a replicated trial of two varieties can support

stimulus.body: A trial of two wheat varieties reports: variety one yielded 2,410 kilograms per hectare across four replicated blocks; variety two yielded 2,655 kilograms per hectare under the same seed rate, sowing date and rainfall. Taste tests of the flour were preferred by 18 of 24 panel members for the second variety, and the second also produced 20 percent less straw.

questions.stem: Your trial record for two wheat varieties shows the data above. What can the trial support?

options.text: That the second variety yielded more under these conditions, and traded straw for grain
That the second variety will always out-yield the first in every district
options.misconception: generalises a one season trial to every place and year

options.text: That the first variety was rejected by tasters, since they preferred the second
options.misconception: conflates a taste preference with a rejection of yield

options.text: That the trial proved the second variety needs less fertiliser than the first
options.misconception: invents a fertiliser comparison the trial never ran

questions.explanation: Replicated blocks under the same sowing and rainfall support a yield difference between the two varieties in that season and setting, and the straw figure shows the trade-off. The trial says nothing about other years, districts or fertiliser rates.
questions.hint: Keep the conditions of the trial in mind.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a conservation act left out
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a species list can leave the habitat exposed

stimulus.body: A reserve audit records that 62 species of plant and 14 species of bird are protected within the boundary, but that the water rights for the wetland are held privately and the reed bed outside the boundary is scheduled for drainage.

questions.stem: Your habitat survey found the newly protected wetland's species listed but its water and reed bed exposed. What does the audit show?

options.text: The reserve is legally secure, because its protection depends only on the species list
options.misconception: assumes a species list makes the site secure

options.text: Protection covers the species but not the wetland they depend on, which remains exposed
The reed bed drainage is a separate matter that has no bearing on the reserve
options.misconception: treats a hydrological threat as unrelated to protection

options.text: Private water rights inside the boundary have already been overruled by the statute
options.misconception: assumes the statute overrode existing private rights

questions.explanation: The statute protects named species, but the water rights and the adjacent reed bed determine whether those species survive, and neither is covered. Protection is only as sound as the habitat around it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statute mentions water at all.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A park act read as a mechanism
questions.learningObjective: Weigh two funding routes for keeping a park protected
questions.stem: Your funding proposal for the national park argues for a permanent endowment rather than an annual grant. Draft the assessment.

options.text: An endowment is better because it guarantees the park can never be closed again
options.misconception: assumes permanent money makes closure impossible

options.text: An annual grant is better because it keeps the park responsive to changing needs
options.misconception: treats flexibility as more important than continuity of staffing

options.text: An endowment secures long-term staffing, while an annual grant keeps costs flexible but uncertain
Both routes are equal, since the money's source never affects the work done
options.misconception: assumes funding source makes no difference to protection

questions.explanation: An endowment pays for rangers and maintenance across the years that decide whether a park survives, while an annual grant allows adjustment but leaves the staff exposed each budget round. Neither removes the need for a political decision.
questions.hint: Think about what happens in a bad budget year.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An agreement with no mechanism behind it
questions.learningObjective: Identify the missing element that keeps an agreement from operating
questions.stem: Your review of the reserve's legal status notes that a widely signed agreement on shared fishery management exists but no body has ever been constituted to run it. What is missing?

options.text: More signatory states, since the agreement needs a larger majority to count
options.misconception: believes the agreement failed for want of signatures

options.text: A shared definition of the fish species covered, since the text names none
options.misconception: fixates on species names rather than the absent machinery

options.text: A newer date of signature, since the original agreement has expired
options.misconception: invents an expiry for an agreement never stated

options.text: An institution with people and money to carry out the agreed actions

questions.explanation: An agreement without a constituted body has nobody to convene meetings, inspect grounds or enforce rules, so its paragraphs stay words on paper. More signatures or a species list will not substitute for an institution with staff and a budget.
questions.hint: Ask who would actually do the agreed work.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A park act read as a mechanism
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the legal status of a reserve affects what a surveyor finds
questions.stem: Explain in a short paragraph how a reserve's legal status changes what a field surveyor will actually find on the ground.

answer.exemplar: A good answer distinguishes a paper designation from a working reserve, noting that a real one has a mapped boundary, a prohibition enforced by staff, settled land rights inside the line and a funded maintenance programme. It adds that in a paper reserve the surveyor will find the same species but also grazing, drainage, hunting and extraction continuing, because nothing has removed those pressures.

questions.explanation: Legal status decides whether boundaries are enforced and land rights settled. A good answer links the documents to what a surveyor will find on the ground.
questions.hint: Separate the paperwork from the pressures.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An agreement with no mechanism behind it
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an agreement in force from one that operates

stimulus.body: A field record for a border wetland states that two neighbouring governments signed an agreement to manage shared migratory habitat, that the agreement has been in force for six years, and that no joint survey, monitoring schedule or meeting has taken place since it was signed.

questions.stem: Your field notebook for the border wetland records the situation above. What does it show?

options.text: The agreement has been legally void for six years because nothing has happened under it
options.misconception: assumes inactivity voids a valid agreement

options.text: The agreement is in force but non-functional, with no machinery behind its words
The wetland is unprotected because the two governments never agreed anything at all
options.misconception: mistakes an unimplemented agreement for no agreement

options.text: The wetland is already well managed, since the agreement gives it legal protection
options.misconception: equates legal status with actual management

questions.explanation: An agreement in force with no survey, monitoring or meeting has no operating mechanism, so the management it promised never happened. Legal protection on paper and protection in the field are different things.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything has actually been done.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A conference that produced only a declaration
questions.learningObjective: Read a summit outcome for the state of its machinery

stimulus.body: The final text of a summit declares a shared commitment to protect mountain forests, states that signatories will report progress every two years, and closes with a paragraph recording that the format for reporting and the body to receive it will be decided later.

questions.stem: Your conference notes summarise a summit that ended with the text above. How should the survey team read it?

options.text: A serious commitment in intent, but one whose reporting machinery is still unwritten
A binding agreement in full, since every state signed the final text
options.misconception: treats signature as proof that obligations are operational

options.text: A diplomatic gesture with no content, since it protects nothing in particular
options.misconception: dismisses a real commitment because of missing detail

options.text: A completed instrument, since the decision to report is itself the reporting system
options.misconception: confuses an intention to report with a working report

questions.explanation: The text commits states to act and to report, but leaves the reporting format and the receiving body unset, so the obligation cannot yet be checked. Signature alone does not complete an instrument whose machinery is undecided.
questions.hint: Separate the promise from the machinery.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The commitment mechanism of a climate treaty
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a commitment mechanism from a shared aspiration
questions.stem: Your briefing note asks what distinguishes a climate treaty's commitment mechanism from a shared aspiration. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: An aspiration names a goal; a mechanism sets targets, reporting duties and a cycle for strengthening them
An aspiration is signed by states; a mechanism is published by a non-governmental group
options.misconception: confuses who speaks with how binding a text is

options.text: An aspiration fixes legal penalties; a mechanism relies on courts to enforce each pledge
options.misconception: invents penalties for a mechanism that carries none

options.text: An aspiration is written in law; a mechanism is kept as an unpublished ministerial note
options.misconception: treats secrecy as the mark of a real mechanism

questions.explanation: A shared aspiration names an outcome, while a working mechanism fixes targets, obliges states to report and requires those targets to be strengthened over time. Signature, penalties or secrecy do not distinguish the two.
questions.hint: Ask what a mechanism actually requires states to do.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commitment and its revision
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a ratchet provision does to a pledged target
questions.stem: Your compliance file shows a country's pledged emissions target for 2025, and a clause requiring each country's next target to be at least as strong as the one before. What does that clause do?

options.text: It caps future targets so that no country is asked to do more than it did before
options.misconception: reads the clause as a ceiling rather than a floor

options.text: It allows a country to lower its target whenever its economy turns down
options.misconception: invents an economic escape clause

options.text: It applies only to countries that have already met their earlier targets
options.misconception: invents a conditional trigger

options.text: It sets a floor under ambition, so each new target must not be weaker

questions.explanation: A clause requiring the next target to be at least as strong sets a floor, so ambition cannot be quietly wound back between rounds. It does not cap effort, excuse a downturn or depend on earlier performance.
questions.hint: Ask whether effort is limited or protected.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the new cereal varieties required
questions.learningObjective: Compare a modern variety with a landrace across input levels

stimulus.body: An extension note records that the short-straw varieties released in the district yielded 1.9 tonnes per hectare with fertiliser and irrigation, but only 0.6 tonnes without either, against 1.4 tonnes from the local landrace under the same management.

questions.stem: Your agronomy trial compares an old landrace with a modern variety under two input levels. What does the note show?

options.text: The modern variety's advantage depends on high inputs and reverses without them
The modern variety is more productive at every level of input tested
options.misconception: ignores the reversed ranking at low inputs

options.text: The landrace is obsolete in every respect, since it lost under both systems
options.misconception: ignores the landrace's result under low inputs

options.text: The two varieties are genetically identical, and the differences came from sampling
options.misconception: invents a sampling explanation for a recorded difference

questions.explanation: The modern variety leads with fertiliser and irrigation but falls behind the landrace without them, so its advantage is conditional on bought inputs rather than built in. That reversal matters for farmers with little cash or water.
questions.hint: Compare the two rankings side by side.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the new cereal varieties required
questions.learningObjective: Apply a variety's input requirements when designing a trial

stimulus.body: A seed department note lists the requirements for the new wheat varieties: sown at the same date as local grain, given two top dressings of fertiliser, threshed within a narrow window, and sold into a graded market that rejects grain of mixed quality.

questions.stem: Your trial design compares two modern cereal varieties against the local check. What does the note imply for the trial?

options.text: The trial can skip fertiliser, because the varieties do not respond to it
options.misconception: denies the response to inputs the note lists

options.text: The trial must apply the stated inputs or it will not test the varieties fairly
The trial should compare varieties only by grain quality, since yield no longer matters
options.misconception: reduces the trial to one measure the note does not limit

options.text: The trial must be run without any local check plot, since the new grain replaces it
options.misconception: assumes the check plot has no comparative value

questions.explanation: Varieties that respond to fertiliser and need timely sowing and a single harvesting window can only be judged under those conditions, so the trial must reproduce them. Dropping inputs or the local check would mislead.
questions.hint: Reproduce the conditions the note sets out.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A trial of two varieties
questions.learningObjective: Propose a design for a fair trial of two cereal varieties
questions.stem: Your trial write-up argues that a fair comparison of two cereal varieties needs a particular design. Draft the proposal.

options.text: Grow both varieties in adjacent strips at one site for a single season and compare
options.misconception: treats one site and season as a fair general comparison

options.text: Ask two experienced farmers which variety they prefer and follow their choice
options.misconception: uses preference rather than measurement as the test

options.text: Replicate both varieties across blocks and sites, use the local landrace as a check
Publish whichever variety wins in the trial with the highest single result
options.misconception: selects for the most flattering outcome rather than the average

questions.explanation: Replication across blocks and sites separates variety effects from soil and season effects, and the local landrace as a check anchors the comparison to what farmers already grow. A single strip or a single best result cannot do that work.
questions.hint: Ask what a single strip cannot rule out.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commitment and its revision
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate how a country should revise a pledged target
questions.stem: Your committee paper weighs whether a country should revise its pledged target upward before the next deadline. Draft the recommendation.

options.text: Revise only after other countries have moved, to keep the ambition level
options.misconception: makes collective action depend on others moving first

options.text: Do not revise, because the original pledge is legally fixed for the whole period
options.misconception: assumes a target can never be strengthened

options.text: Revise only if domestic prices rise, so that firms can afford the change
options.misconception: makes climate pledges turn on short term prices

options.text: Revise upward, since a cycle that permits strengthening only undercuts the treaty

questions.explanation: A ratchet exists so that pledges get stronger over time; if a country waits for others or for convenient prices, the cycle becomes a licence to stand still. Revision should follow the direction the mechanism was built to enforce.
questions.hint: Ask what the mechanism is for.

questions.topic: What a conservation act left out
questions.learningObjective: Recognise an interest omitted from a conservation statute
questions.stem: A protected wetland's listing was justified on grounds of rare bird breeding, and the statute protects birds and prohibits hunting in their roosts. Which interest is left out?

options.text: The fishers and reed cutters whose livelihoods depend on the same wetland
The hunters, whose use of the roosts the statute prohibits outright
options.misconception: treats a prohibited activity as an omitted interest

options.text: The birds that winter elsewhere but pass over the wetland each autumn
options.misconception: assumes migratory visitors fall inside a breeding protection

options.text: The park wardens, whose own authority the statute is meant to strengthen
options.misconception: reads the statute's beneficiaries as the omitted interest

questions.topic: An agreement with no mechanism behind it
questions.learningObjective: Read the operative status of a signed agreement with an unfinished annex

stimulus.body: A note records that twenty-two states signed a migratory species agreement, that the list of protected species is printed in an annex, and that the annex is marked provisional pending review, with no body appointed to conduct that review.

questions.stem: Your diplomatic file records the agreement above. What follows from the note?

options.text: Twenty-two signatures have made the agreement fully enforceable against the parties
options.misconception: assumes signatures alone create complete obligations

options.text: The protected list is unfinished, so what the agreement requires stays uncertain
The agreement is void because the annex carries no signatures of its own
options.misconception: requires a separate signature on an annex

options.text: The agreement protects nothing until a review body is appointed, which may take years
options.misconception: says the existing terms protect nothing whatever

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A park act read as a mechanism
questions.learningObjective: Identify the mechanism a park statute must supply
questions.stem: A park statute created a reserve but supplied only a prohibition on hunting. Which mechanism is missing?

options.text: A prohibition on mining and quarrying within the reserve boundaries
options.misconception: answers a different question about which act to ban

options.text: A visitor levy to fund the paths, wardens and maintenance the park needs
options.misconception: confuses a funding source with the missing mechanism

options.text: An enforcing staff and a budget, so that the prohibition can be applied
A map of the boundary so that visitors know where the reserve begins
options.misconception: treats signage as the essential missing piece

questions.explanation: A prohibition with nobody to enforce it and no money to pay for that enforcement is a sentence in a statute rather than a working protection. Boundary maps and additional bans help, but staff and funding make any ban operative.

questions.topic: A conference that produced only a declaration
questions.learningObjective: Judge a conference by the machinery behind its declarations

stimulus.body: A conference's outcomes document lists six declarations, two of which name bodies to be created and budgets to be set, and four of which state intentions without naming any body, money or date. A footnote records that only the two funded declarations have produced any activity.

questions.stem: Your summit report describes a meeting that produced the outcomes above. What should the survey team conclude?

options.text: The conference failed, since most of its declarations were never implemented
options.misconception: judges the whole meeting by its weakest outcomes

options.text: The conference succeeded, because two well funded declarations were adopted
options.misconception: judges the whole meeting by its strongest outcomes

options.text: The declarations were legally binding, and the lack of activity proves breach
options.misconception: confuses non-implementation with legal breach

options.text: Declarations with bodies and budgets moved, while the rest stayed as words

questions.explanation: The two declarations that named a body and money produced activity, while the four without either produced none, which points to machinery rather than will as the difference. Neither blanket success nor blanket failure is supported.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The commitment mechanism of a climate treaty
questions.learningObjective: State what a target-based commitment requires of each state
questions.stem: A climate treaty's first commitment period required each state to set its own emissions target and to report on progress every two years. What does this arrangement rest on?

options.text: National plans and honest reporting, since the treaty cannot set each country's path
A global engineering model that allocates each state's emissions budget
options.misconception: invents a centrally allocated budget of emissions

options.text: Trade penalties applied to any state whose progress report disappoints
options.misconception: invents penalties for a reporting duty

options.text: Third-party certification of every state report before it counts at all
options.misconception: invents a certification step the arrangement lacks

questions.explanation: Nationally set targets with periodic reporting work through each state's own policies, plans and honesty. Central allocation, penalties and third-party certification are not part of this arrangement.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commitment and its revision
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a revised target from a rephrased one
questions.stem: A country's revised target is more ambitious than its first, yet it covers a different base year. Why must the two be compared carefully?

options.text: Because a stronger target on a later base year can still mean a slower real reduction
Because the base year determines what each percentage is measured from
options.misconception: treats a rebased target as automatically more demanding

options.text: Because base years change the reporting schedule for every other state
options.misconception: invents a reporting consequence for other states

options.text: Because only the first base year was agreed, and later ones are void
options.misconception: asserts that rebasing voids the earlier commitment

questions.explanation: A percentage means little until the base year is fixed, so a stronger-looking number can describe a slower actual cut when measured against the earlier starting point. Comparing the two requires putting both on the same base.
questions.hint: Put both numbers on one starting point.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the new cereal varieties required
questions.learningObjective: Explain the risks the new cereal varieties shifted onto farmers
questions.stem: Prepare a short explanation for the district officer of what risks the new cereal varieties shifted from the state onto individual farmers.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that the new varieties gave higher yields only where farmers could buy fertiliser, irrigation and improved seed on time, so their fortunes turned on cash flow and on timely delivery. It adds that a single epidemic or a failed payment could wipe out a season for a household with no landrace in reserve, and that the loss was borne privately rather than by the state.

questions.explanation: Higher yields came with cash costs and dependence on bought inputs and a graded market, so a bad season now lands on the household rather than the state. A good answer names the input costs and the loss of a fallback.
questions.hint: Ask who carries the loss in a bad season.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A trial of two varieties
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features of a randomised block trial design

stimulus.body: A trial note records that two barley varieties were sown on 24 plots arranged in four blocks of six, with each variety appearing once in every block, that sowing and fertiliser were identical across blocks, and that a third plot in each block carried the local landrace.

questions.stem: Your trial protocol requires each plot to be comparable. What does the design note show?

options.text: A randomised block design with a local check, so variety effects can be separated
A design strong enough to guarantee the same result in every other season
options.misconception: treats a good design as immunity to other conditions

options.text: A design that measures only the two new varieties, ignoring older grain
options.misconception: ignores the landrace plots in the note

options.text: A design in which each block received different fertiliser to test response
options.misconception: reverses the note on what was held constant

questions.explanation: Placing each variety once in every block and holding sowing and fertiliser constant lets differences within a block separate variety from soil and season, and the landrace plots anchor the result to local practice. It does not guarantee the same outcome elsewhere.
questions.hint: Ask what the blocks control for.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A trial of two varieties
questions.learningObjective: Read a trial log for a second advantage beyond yield

stimulus.body: A trial log records that the shorter-straw variety was sprayed once for rust and that the taller local variety needed spraying twice in the same season, and that both were sown on the same day with the same fertiliser.

questions.stem: Your trial record shows yields for two cereal varieties and their spray schedules. What does the log show?

options.text: The taller variety's lower yield came from a heavier rust burden, not from any trait of the seed
options.misconception: attributes a yield gap to disease alone

options.text: The shorter variety needed less spraying as well as giving more straw, a second advantage
The spray counts show the local variety was grown on better land, not better seed
options.misconception: invents a land difference the identical blocks exclude

options.text: Spraying costs should be added to the taller variety's yield to make the comparison fair
options.misconception: adds a cost the trial did not measure

questions.explanation: On the same sown land with the same fertiliser, the shorter-straw variety needed one spray against two, so it carried lower disease management cost as well as giving more straw. That is a second advantage, not a confounder.
questions.hint: Count the sprays for each variety.

options.misconception: measures only what the statute already protects

options.text: Ask wardens whether they think the reserve is working well
options.misconception: uses official opinion rather than field measurement

options.text: Measure water levels, reed extent and the livelihoods of users beside the boundary
Wait for a decade of records before drawing any conclusion at all
options.misconception: treats delay as a method rather than a cost

questions.explanation: A bird count alone would record the protection working while the habitat fails, so the survey must also track water, reeds and the pressures from users just outside the boundary. That is where the omitted interests show up.

questions.stem: Your legal notes record the park's annual report above. Which part of the reserve is least secure?

options.text: The ranger establishment, because 14 rangers cannot cover 62 kilometres of boundary
options.misconception: treats a staffing level as a legal weakness

options.text: The maintenance budget, because trails and gatehouses fall outside the legal protection
options.misconception: confuses upkeep spending with legal security

options.text: The surveyed boundary, because a surveyed line can be moved by later agreement
options.misconception: assumes a surveyed boundary lacks legal force

options.text: The three villages whose land titles remain unsettled inside the protected boundary

questions.explanation: Unsettled titles mean residents keep rights that the statute assumes are extinguished, so protection faces dispute from within the line. Staffing and maintenance bear on the quality of protection, not on whether the land is legally secured.

questions.stem: Explain in a short paragraph why creating a national park changes less than its name suggests.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that a designation on paper settles nothing by itself: the boundary must be drawn, land rights inside it extinguished or bought out, prohibitions enforced by paid staff, and the site funded for years. It adds that pressure from outside often continues unchanged, so that a park's fate is decided by the machinery of tenure, staff and budget rather than by the statute's language.

questions.explanation: A designation is only the first step: boundaries, tenure, staff and funding determine whether it works. A good answer shows how each missing piece leaves the pressure unchanged.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen after the paper is signed.

options.misconception: ranks treaties by membership rather than machinery

options.text: It is functioning, since reporting, a standing body and funding are all in place
It is weak, because a convention can never be made to work without new laws
options.misconception: assumes new domestic legislation is always required

options.text: It is unfinished, because no global body has yet approved its reports
options.misconception: invents a global approval step the review does not mention

questions.explanation: A convention becomes functional when its reporting schedule is actually met, its committee meets and its money is confirmed for years ahead, all of which the review records. Party numbers and any global sign-off do not decide the question.

A treaty concluded, since the delegations agreed a text in principle
options.misconception: treats agreement in principle as a concluded treaty

options.text: A failure, since the delegations disagreed about the text throughout
options.misconception: reports disagreement on text that was in fact agreed

options.text: A binding agreement deferred, since only the monitoring details were left open
options.misconception: narrows the gap to monitoring alone

questions.explanation: The delegations agreed the text but could not settle monitoring, funding or reporting, so what emerged was a statement of principles with no machinery behind it. Agreement in principle is not a treaty, and the gap was wider than monitoring.

options.misconception: invents a centrally allocated budget

options.text: A tariff schedule that penalises imports from countries with weak targets
options.misconception: invents trade penalties for climate pledges

options.text: A cycle of reported national targets that must not weaken between rounds
An independent inspection of every country's power stations each year
options.misconception: invents inspection of facilities

questions.stem: Your revision watch records that a country moved its 2030 target from a 25 percent reduction to a 40 percent reduction against its 2010 level. What does that revision signal?

options.misconception: reads a tighter target as slack in the old one

options.text: That the country's technology has changed so much that the earlier figure is void
options.misconception: treats a revision as invalidating the previous pledge

options.misconception: assumes the base year changed when only the target did

options.text: That the state accepted a steeper reduction against an unchanged baseline

questions.stem: Write a short analysis for the extension service describing what farmers needed in order to adopt the new cereal varieties successfully.

answer.exemplar: A good answer lists the linked requirements: certified seed bought before sowing, fertiliser delivered on credit and in time, water where the season was unreliable, a harvesting window tight enough to meet, and a market that would grade and pay for a uniform grain. It adds that extension advice and a clean break from the old seed were both needed, since a mixed harvest could not be sold at the graded price.

questions.explanation: Adoption required seed, fertiliser, water, timely harvesting and a graded market, plus advice and a clear break from the old seed. A good answer shows these requirements were linked in time as well as in cash.
questions.hint: List what had to be arranged before sowing.

questions.topic: A trial of two varieties

stimulus.body: Plot instructions for a cereal trial state that each variety must be sown at the same date and seed rate, that plots must be separated by a discard strip, and that harvesting must be done for each plot separately so that every plot's yield can be weighed.

questions.stem: Your trial protocol requires each plot to be comparable. Why does the instruction to harvest separately matter?

options.text: It lets the trial be run by different teams in different fields
options.misconception: invents a staffing reason for a measurement rule

options.text: It reduces the cost of harvesting by avoiding the need for weighbridges
options.misconception: confuses careful measurement with lower cost

options.text: It prevents mixing between plots and makes each plot's yield measurable
It allows the trial to continue into a second season without replanting
options.misconception: invents a seasonal consequence

questions.explanation: Harvesting each plot separately stops grain from one treatment mixing into another and makes each plot's yield a real measurement rather than an average. Without it, the comparison cannot be trusted.
questions.hint: Ask what happens if the plots share a harvest.

questions.learningObjective: Weigh two ways of protecting a park's boundary

options.text: Hardened boundaries are better because they remove the need for any rangers at all
options.misconception: claims physical barriers replace personnel

options.text: Hardened boundaries cut incursions cheaply but need upkeep and still need people to enforce
Patrol-only protection is better because it never damages the habitat it protects
options.misconception: assumes patrols leave no trace

options.text: Hardened boundaries are better because they make the park immune to pressure from outside
options.misconception: treats a fence as a complete answer to outside pressure

questions.learningObjective: Identify the omission in a conservation statute's stated purpose
questions.stem: A reserve's protection is said to depend on a statute that names the preservation of rare plants and the prohibition of collecting them. What does that statute omit?

options.text: The protection of the soils and waters on which those rare plants depend
options.misconception: thinks a plant list is enough for the whole habitat

options.text: The prohibition on picking the plants, which the statute sets out clearly
options.misconception: points to a duty the statute plainly includes

options.text: The control of drainage and grazing that threatens the plants in practice
The funding for wardens, which every such statute must be read to include
options.misconception: assumes a funding clause the statute never mentions

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish weak will from missing machinery in an agreement

options.text: The agreement is invalid because the commission reached no decisions in two meetings
options.misconception: treats an unproductive meeting as voiding a treaty

options.text: The commission cannot act because the four states disagree about the catch limit
options.misconception: confuses a disagreement of members with a missing institution

options.text: The machinery exists but has not yet produced the agreed management it was set up for
The four states have no need for a shared limit, since each controls its own waters
options.misconception: denies the need for the body the states themselves created

questions.explanation: A commission with seats and meetings is the machinery, and it has simply not yet produced a catch limit or any inspection, which is a failure of agreement or will rather than of structure. Meetings without decisions do not void the agreement.

options.misconception: claims a staffing arrangement the extract omits

options.text: A complete legal framework, since every necessary element appears in the text
options.misconception: treats a list of clauses as a working system

options.text: Only a prohibition, since the fund and the timber rules are merely advisory
options.misconception: downgrades binding clauses to advice

options.text: A prohibition and a sum of money, with the boundary and the staff left to be made

options.misconception: invents a compliance standard the text lacks

options.text: The commitment binds only the states that later settle the definition
options.misconception: narrows the binding parties without cause

options.misconception: mistakes a record for the means of protection

options.misconception: claims a legal effect for peer review

options.text: Because review panels can fine states that miss their targets
options.misconception: invents fines for a peer review system

options.text: Because reporting makes progress visible, which changes what states will choose to do
Because reviewed states receive foreign aid linked to their reported performance
options.misconception: invents aid conditionality for a reporting duty

options.misconception: treats replacement as cancellation of the old obligation

questions.topic: What a conservation act left out

questions.stem: Explain in a short note why early conservation acts typically protected a narrow list of species while leaving the pressures behind them alone.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that such acts grew out of hunting and collecting complaints, so they named the visible and marketable targets, birds, eggs and certain big animals, and left drainage, grazing and enclosure unmentioned. It notes that the pressure was therefore often unchanged, and that the partial protection could even protect one species by displacing the pressure onto another.

questions.explanation: Early acts grew from hunting and collecting complaints, so they named the visible targets and left the underlying pressures untouched. A good answer notes that pressure could then fall on other species.
questions.hint: Ask which complaints started these laws.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An agreement with no mechanism behind it
questions.learningObjective: State the current legal position of a signed but unratified convention

stimulus.body: A diplomatic note records that a convention on shared marine protection was signed by nineteen states, that its entry into force required a stated number of ratifications that had not yet been reached, and that an annex of protected areas was scheduled to be drawn up only after entry into force.

questions.stem: Your treaty file notes that the convention above has not entered into force. What is the current position?

options.text: The convention is already binding on all nineteen signatories in practice
options.misconception: assumes signature binds immediately

options.text: The annex will be ready soon, because it can be drafted before entry into force
options.misconception: ignores the stated sequence of drafting after entry

options.text: It is signed but not yet in force, and its protected areas have not yet been defined
The convention has failed, because nineteen signatures were fewer than required
options.misconception: treats a pending threshold as a failure

questions.explanation: The note is explicit: the ratifications needed for entry into force have not arrived, and the annex is to follow entry into force, so no areas are defined yet. Signature binds intentions, not the obligations that wait on entry into force.
questions.hint: Follow the note's own sequence.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A conference that produced only a declaration
questions.learningObjective: Assess a summit outcome with an announced but unallocated fund

stimulus.body: A conference's final act records that delegations adopted a declaration on forest protection, that a support fund was announced for the following year, and that the fund's size, source and disbursement rules were left to be determined by the secretariat.

questions.stem: Your summit report describes a meeting that produced the final act above. What should the survey team conclude?

options.text: A complete package, because a fund has been announced for the following year
options.misconception: treats an announcement as a funded mechanism

options.text: A shared political commitment with a real gap, since the money is unallocated
A failure, since no money at all was promised for forest protection
options.misconception: reads an unallocated fund as no fund

options.text: A binding treaty, because the secretariat was given duties to carry out
options.misconception: reads administrative tasks as treaty obligations

questions.explanation: The declaration carries the political commitment and the announcement of a fund shows intent, but size, source and disbursement rules are all outstanding, so the money cannot yet reach anyone. Delegating the detail to a secretariat is not the same as settling it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the money can yet be paid out.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The commitment mechanism of a climate treaty
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an international pledge becomes a domestic duty
questions.stem: Your treaty analysis identifies the mechanism that turns an international pledge into something a ministry must actually do. What is that link?

options.text: An international body inspects national ministries and publishes rankings
options.misconception: invents ministry inspections for treaty compliance

options.text: A court in the country of the treaty orders the ministry to comply
options.misconception: invents a domestic court order for an international pledge

options.text: The ministry's budget is set abroad by the treaty secretariat each year
options.misconception: describes foreign budget control that does not exist

options.text: National law, plans and budgets carry the target, so the pledge lands on domestic policy

questions.explanation: A target binds a state only when its own law, plans, budgets and regulations implement it, and that is where reporting obligations then bite. Inspection, court orders and foreign budget control are not the link.
questions.hint: Ask who writes the regulations.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commitment and its revision
questions.learningObjective: Compare three kinds of revision to a pledged target

stimulus.body: A watch list records that one country tightened its 2030 target from 35 to 42 percent below its 2019 level, a second country kept its target but moved the baseline from 2025 to 2030, and a third country dropped its target by 5 percent with no explanation.

questions.stem: Your revision watch records these three changes. Which comparison is most informative?

options.text: Only the first change matters, because the other two are not genuine revisions
options.misconception: dismisses rebasing and weakening as non revisions

options.text: The first tightens on a stable baseline, the second rebases, and the third weakens
The third country's change is the most ambitious, because it reduced the target
options.misconception: reads a lower reduction as greater ambition

options.text: All three changes are equivalent, because each concerned a percentage figure
options.misconception: ignores baseline and direction

questions.explanation: The three changes differ in kind: one raises ambition on the same base, one moves the base so the number looks different, and one simply lowers ambition. Comparing them requires holding the baseline and the direction in view.
questions.hint: Check base and direction for each.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the new cereal varieties required
questions.learningObjective: Read yields across water regimes to test a variety's advantage

stimulus.body: A harvest account shows the new wheat variety yielding 2.2 tonnes per hectare on the irrigated block, 1.3 on the block with only one watering, and 0.7 on the unirrigated block, against 1.1 for the landrace on the unirrigated block.

questions.stem: Your trial ledger shows yields for two cereal varieties across three water regimes. What does the account show?

options.text: The new variety's yield falls sharply as water falls, and the landrace beats it when dry
The new variety is superior in every condition, so water makes no difference
options.misconception: ignores the declining yields across the blocks

options.text: The landrace is the better variety because it wins on the unirrigated block alone
options.misconception: judges both varieties on one block

options.text: The three blocks show that rainfall rather than irrigation set the results
options.misconception: misattributes the treatment to weather

questions.explanation: The new variety drops from 2.2 to 0.7 tonnes as water is withdrawn, and the unirrigated landrace at 1.1 tonnes beats it there. The new variety's advantage is conditional on reliable water, which matters greatly in a dry season.
questions.hint: Read the three blocks in order.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A trial of two varieties
questions.learningObjective: Identify what makes a trial comparison defensible
questions.stem: Your trial report argues that a defensible comparison of two cereal varieties requires several features. Which set is right?

options.text: Many varieties, few plots and one harvest, to concentrate the effort
options.misconception: reverses the requirements for replication and variety number

options.text: Small plots, one site and the growers' own choice of seed
options.misconception: sacrifices control for grower preference

options.text: Replicated plots, a comparison treatment and conditions held equal across plots
A long run of seasons, since no single trial can ever prove anything
options.misconception: replaces replication with duration alone

questions.explanation: A defensible comparison needs replication, a comparison treatment and equal conditions across plots, so that a measured difference can be attributed to the variety. Many varieties, tiny plots and one harvest weaken the test rather than strengthen it.
questions.hint: Ask what would let a difference be attributed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A park act read as a mechanism
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a marked boundary with few breaches can still fail

stimulus.body: An inspection reports that the reserve's boundary is marked with posts every fifty metres, that the wardens' round takes nine days to cover the perimeter, and that two breaches of the timber rules were recorded in the last year.

questions.stem: Your reserve inspection found that protection on paper meets little enforcement in practice. What does the report show?

options.text: That the boundary posts are too closely spaced to be maintained
options.misconception: faults the spacing rather than the coverage

options.text: That marking and rules exist, but the patrol frequency leaves gaps to exploit
That the timber rules were too severe, since two breaches were recorded
options.misconception: reads enforcement as evidence of over regulation

options.text: That wardens should be replaced by a longer boundary fence
options.misconception: prescribes fencing without addressing patrol frequency

questions.explanation: A marked boundary and written rules are present, but a nine day round over that perimeter leaves long unsupervised gaps, which is where the recorded breaches occurred. The shortfall is coverage, not the rules themselves.
questions.hint: Compare the round with the perimeter.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a conservation act left out
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a conservation act's omissions should be corrected
questions.stem: Your case for the park tells a funder what the statute leaves out and what that costs. Draft the case.

options.text: The statute should be replaced entirely, because partial protection never works
options.misconception: demands replacement where amendment would do

options.text: The omissions are unimportant, because the listed species are the ones that matter
options.misconception: treats a statutory list as a judgement of value

options.text: No action is needed, because the pressures are the same everywhere in the district
options.misconception: assumes uniform pressure across the district

options.text: Protecting habitat and users alongside the species would close the gap the statute leaves

questions.explanation: The listed species are protected while the habitat and the local users are not, and that gap is where the losses happen. Extending the statute to habitat and to how people use the site closes it without discarding what already works.
questions.hint: Show where the gap does its damage.
